title: Exact lexicographic scheduling and approximate rescheduling
contribution: Two-stage robust P||Cmax in which a lexicographically optimal plan plus binding-decision recovery gets a tight price of robustness (2 for one perturbation, O(f(1+k/(m-k))(f+k)(1+delta/m)) for many) where an arbitrary optimal plan gets Omega(m); with a vectorial-bound LexOpt branch-and-bound (read: arXiv v3).
problem_entry: Price of robustness for P||Cmax called an open question; two-stage recovery with bounded modification of the nominal schedule (pp. 1-5).
key_idea: LexOpt planning imposes optimal substructure (Lemma 4) that makes LPT recovery of free jobs provably good; stage-1 LexOpt solved by branch-and-bound with fractional pseudo-schedule vectorial bounds (pp. 9-15).
assumptions: Uncertainty set U(f,k,delta): at most k unstable jobs beyond factor f, delta surplus machines; recovery keeps all binding job-machine assignments (pp. 3, 9, 13).
proof_devices: strong NP-hardness of the recovery problem (Theorem 2, p. 13)
degenerate-instance lower bound Omega(m) for arbitrary optimal plans (Theorem 3, p. 14)
optimal-substructure lemma for LexOpt schedules (Lemma 4, pp. 14-15; Lemma 5, p. 16)
per-perturbation-type guarantees composed in a fixed order (Table 1, p. 17; Theorem 5 Type-1 proof pp. 18-19)
vectorial lower/upper bounds via fractional pseudo-schedules (Algorithms 1-2, Lemmas 2-3, pp. 10-12)
experiments: CPLEX/Gurobi via Pyomo; well-formed instances (3 sizes x 3 distributions) and degenerate instances at the phase transition kappa* = log2 m/(m-1); performance profiles vs sequential, weighting and highest-rank-objective methods; scatter of plan closeness to LexOpt vs recovered makespan (pp. 19-23, 44-46).
positioning: Extends recoverable robustness (Liebchen et al.) and price of robustness (Bertsimas-Sim) to P||Cmax; adapts existing LexOpt methods as rivals (pp. 2-5, 20).
writing: Positive/negative result pairing announced in the contributions paragraph; proofs split between main text and a supplement (pp. 5-6).
limits_future: B&B converges on only >30% of intermediate/hard instances; highest-rank heuristic gives best primal results; extensions to facility location and network design (pp. 21, 24).

method_links.note: Exploited structure is the optimal substructure imposed by choosing a LexOpt plan, not structure detected in a user's model.
Three rival exact LexOpt methods adapted and run under one tolerance and time limit; performance profiles; phase-transition-calibrated degenerate instances; own-method timeouts reported.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: lexicographic first stage as a robustness device
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: LexOpt plan gives tight price of robustness 2 vs Omega(m) for an arbitrary optimal plan; recovered quality improves as plan approaches LexOpt (also S079).

transferable: Generate hard instances at a known phase-transition threshold and report them separately from easy ones (pp. 19, 44-45).
Draw a pool of diverse near-optimal plans from the solver's solution pool and scatter normalised plan quality against normalised recovered quality (pp. 21-23).
Pair each positive guarantee with a degenerate instance showing the failure without the structural choice (Theorems 3-4, pp. 14-15).
coauthors: Dimitrios Letsios (KCL, first author), Miten Mistry (Imperial)

quotes.text: Faced with the lack of strong lower bounding techniques for LexOpt scheduling, we develop a new branch-and-bound algorithm, based on vectorial bounds.
Numerical results with randomly generated instances demonstrate that the closest to LexOpt the initial solution is, the better the recovered solution quality we get.

title: A disjunctive cut strengthening technique for convex MINLP
contribution: Strengthens ESH/OA-type cuts for convex MINLP over an exclusive-selection disjunction by solving one small convex NLP per disjunct, giving a single-RHS cut and a dominating per-disjunct-RHS cut that cut geometric-mean iterations from 94 to 39 on big-M MINLPLib and p_ball instances.
problem_entry: OA/ECP/ESH speed depends on outer-approximation tightness; ESH cuts are not supporting hyperplanes of the integer hull, worst for big-M disjunctions (pp. 1-4).
key_idea: Per-disjunct NLPs max alpha'x with x_i = 1 give RHS values b_i; ST uses max b_i, MT uses sum b_i x_i; infeasible disjuncts fix x_i = 0; Rule 1 picks the selection constraint by variable connections (pp. 6-10).
assumptions: Convex C1 constraints, compact linear set, Slater, at least one exclusive-selection constraint; continuous NLPs assumed cheap relative to MILP relaxations (pp. 3-4).
proof_devices: validity of single-tightened cut from optimality of the disjunctive program (Proposition 1, p. 7)
validity of multi-tightened cut by contradiction via exclusivity (Theorem 1, p. 7)
dominance via b_i = z* - Delta_i, Delta_i >= 0 (Theorem 2, pp. 7-8)
infeasible disjunct NLP implies variable fixing (Proposition 2, p. 8)
epsilon right-hand-side relaxation for NLP inexactness (p. 11)
experiments: Basic ESH (MATLAB/OPTI, IPOPT, Gurobi) on 43 big-M instances (clay, flay, slay, sssd, tls, stockcycle, p_ball), 2 h limit (96 h stockcycle); ESH vs ESH+ST vs ESH+MT, plus big-M vs hull vs big-M+MT; rsyn/syn no-gain reported (pp. 14-19).
positioning: Alternative to lift-and-project and separation-based disjunctive cuts (Stubbs-Mehrotra, Ceria-Soares, Trespalacios-Grossmann); same idea as tighter big-M for GDP (pp. 2, 11).
writing: Running toy example EX1 with figures for each cut and each integer assignment; computational trade-off stated explicitly against separation cuts (pp. 5-12).
limits_future: Preliminary proof of concept; NLPs not parallelised; separation cuts can be stronger; little effect on hull formulations or easy linear disjunctions; applicable to OA, ECP, GBD (pp. 11-19).

method_links.note: Big-M (weak) and hull (heavy) treated as two extremes; MT cut on big-M compared with both on the same instances.
Exclusive-selection constraints identified as the disjunctive structure; Rule 1 chooses by direct and step-one connections.
Judged in a deliberately stripped-down ESH as a proof of concept, not inside a full solver.
No-gain classes (rsyn, syn) reported with averages.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: decompose the hull into independent per-disjunct subproblems in the original space
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Per-disjunct convex NLPs replace the lifted perspective formulation, avoid division by zero, parallelise and detect infeasible disjuncts.

transferable: Solve |D| small per-disjunct problems in the original space instead of the lifted hull problem (pp. 6, 11).
Design cuts so numerical error enters only the right-hand side, then relax by epsilon (p. 11).
Publish a parametrisable synthetic family (p_ball: balls x points x dimension) next to library instances (pp. 14, 27).
Report the cut on the weak formulation against both weak and strong formulations (Table 3, p. 18).
Count variables fixed as a side effect and check that LP-based bounds tightening cannot fix them (p. 15).

quotes.text: These are preliminary results and are mainly intended as a proof of concept.
Therefore, the trade-off of our cut strengthening approach is a reduced computational complexity at the expense of a possibly weaker cut.

title: Approximate and robust bounded job start scheduling for Royal Mail delivery offices
contribution: Introduces bounded job start scheduling from Royal Mail van gates, with LPT tightly 2-approximate, 5/3 on long and optimal on short instances, a 1.985-approximate long-short mixing algorithm, and a lexicographic two-stage robust approach scored by van augmentation on 300 real instances (read: arXiv v2).
problem_entry: Royal Mail van exit gate bounds job starts per time unit; fixed working day makes makespan-based price of robustness unsuitable, so robustness is measured by extra vans (pp. 2, 4-5).
key_idea: Split instances into long/short classes, prove per-class ratios, then run both classes in parallel (LSM); robust stage 1 lexicographically minimises job completion times plus theta x vans, stage 2 keeps start times (pp. 5, 15-17, 21-23).
assumptions: Integer processing times, identical machines, analysis for g = 1 (justified by discretisation), m >= 7 for LSM, perturbation factor F; B = 2 and theta chosen empirically (pp. 5, 15, 20-22).
proof_devices: Omega(log n) integrality gap of the natural IP (Theorem 2, p. 8)
concave relaxation bounding idle machine time before the last job start (pp. 3, 5)
long/short instance classification with per-class LPT ratios (Theorems 4-5, pp. 12, 14)
experiments: 300 instances from three delivery offices (15-min discretisation, g from data); heuristics for m in [5, 50]; MILP vs historical schedules saves at least 10/25/10 vans per day; +/-50% processing-time noise robustness scatter (pp. 23-32).
positioning: Relates BJSP to P||Cmax, forbidden-set and forbidden-start-time scheduling; adapts the authors' S052 LexOpt approach with machine augmentation (pp. 3-6, 19-21).
writing: Industrial context with network numbers first, then a two-fold contribution statement; long list of open questions in the conclusion (pp. 2, 32-33).
limits_future: Robust approach only empirical, price of robustness open; sub-2 ratio without augmentation open; vehicle sharing across offices and vehicle routing as directions (pp. 32-33).

method_links.note: Baseline is the partner's historical practice rather than rival solvers; the gap to practice is the headline.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: lexicographic first stage as a robustness device
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Lex-min of job completion times plus van count as stage-1 objective; lower characteristic value gives fewer vans after recovery (with S052).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: approximation algorithms for process systems engineering
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Paper framed as part of 'larger aims towards approximation algorithms for process systems engineering'; greedy heuristics with guarantees adoptable by practitioners.

transferable: When the partner's objective is fixed by the business, measure robustness in the resource the partner can buy (vans) (pp. 4-5, 20-21).
Classify instances by a threshold tied to the machine count, prove per-class ratios, then design an algorithm that mixes the classes (pp. 5, 15).
Check real data for the share of each theoretical class before optimising for one (pp. 24-25).
coauthors: Dimitrios Letsios (KCL, first author), Jeremy T. Bradley (Royal Mail), Suraj G, Natasha Page (Imperial)

quotes.text: Furthermore, any Royal Mail instance can be converted to g = 1 using small discretization.
This finding is a strong indication that more efficient fleet management might be possible in Royal Mail delivery offices.

title: Design of dynamic experiments for black-box model discrimination
contribution: Extends analytical design of dynamic experiments for model discrimination to process, control, initial-state and parameter uncertainty, and to black-box dynamic models by placing GP surrogates on the one-step state transition (read: arXiv v2, titled 'Using Gaussian Processes to Design Dynamic Experiments for Black-Box Model Discrimination under Uncertainty').
problem_entry: Rival mechanistic models often all fit existing data; industrial models in legacy code have no gradients; analytical vs Monte Carlo design split (abstract, pp. 1-3).
key_idea: GP prior on (x_k, u_k, theta) -> x_{k+1} keeps surrogate input dimension independent of horizon; Taylor moment propagation with GP gradients; a third mode uses the true black box for means and the GP only for gradients (pp. 8-10, 18).
assumptions: Gaussian noises and parameter posterior (Laplace), known noise covariances, first-order state-space form, linear observation map, open-loop design; linearisation admitted for tractability (pp. 7, 17-18).
experiments: Yeast fermentation case (Espie-Macchietto; constants Chen-Asprey): published optima reproduced and improved by 7.8%/8%; mean vs cone constraints over 25 simulations with 100-sample Monte Carlo violation levels; control-covariance misspecification 2x2; GP surrogates marginally worse than analytical (pp. 12-17).
positioning: Hybridises analytical (Chen-Asprey style) and data-driven design, extending Olofsson et al. ICML 2018 from static to dynamic models (abstract, pp. 3, 18-19).
writing: Opens with a three-panel toy figure (step, random, optimised control) showing why naive inputs fail to discriminate (pp. 2-3).
limits_future: Linearisation and GP errors accumulate over long horizons; prior covariance shrunk to make the first experiment feasible; closed-loop design too costly; future advanced GPs and hybrid mechanistic/data-driven models (pp. 17-19).

method_links.note: Learned surrogate embedded in the optimisation problem, but as a smooth GP feeding local gradients rather than piecewise structure solved globally.
Published optima re-evaluated with the original criterion before extending; Monte Carlo verification of constraint violations.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: reproduce the classic published instance before extending
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Espie-Macchietto optimum recovered from perturbed starts; Chen-Asprey objective recomputed (2601 vs 2805) with the gap attributed to 20 years of solver progress.

transferable: Learn the one-step transition map, not the trajectory map, to keep surrogate input dimension fixed over long horizons (p. 18).
Re-solve the classic published instance under the original formulation and report both objectives before claiming improvement (p. 13).
Cross modelled vs true uncertainty (small/large x small/large) and report success, failure and inconclusive rates separately (p. 16).
coauthors: Simon Olofsson (first author), Eduardo S. Schultz, Adel Mhamdi, Alexander Mitsos (RWTH Aachen), Marc Peter Deisenroth (UCL)

quotes.text: Since the problem formulation is identical, we assume this discrepancy is due to the improvement in optimisation solvers after 20 years.
Hence, we are punished less for conservative estimates of the control covariance than for overly optimistic estimates.

title: Multi-objective constrained optimization for energy applications via tree ensembles
contribution: Extends ENTMOOT to constrained multi-objective black-box optimisation by combining tree-ensemble MIP encodings, a distance/similarity exploration term and a weighted Chebyshev acquisition, outperforming NSGA-II on synthetic, wind-farm and battery-design benchmarks (read: arXiv v1).
problem_entry: Energy design problems are expensive black boxes with multiple objectives, categorical inputs and explicit input constraints; evolutionary methods are sample-hungry and handle constraints poorly (pp. 2-4).
key_idea: Weighted Chebyshev scalarisation of normalised tree-ensemble predictions minus kappa x exploration, single-levelled by an epigraph variable; solved as a nonconvex MIQP with input constraints so proposals are feasible (pp. 9-10, 14).
assumptions: Black-box evaluation dominates cost; observed min/max normalisation unless bounds given; 400 trees depth 3, kappa = 1.96 fixed across runs; 100 s Gurobi limit once feasible (pp. 10, 15-16).
experiments: Synthetic bi-objective benchmarks (GD, IGD, MPFE, VR vs NSGA-II-approximated true fronts); 16-turbine wind farm and PyBaMM battery design (bounded hypervolume); 25 fixed seeds, identical initial points, medians and quartiles (pp. 15-29).
positioning: Builds on ENTMOOT (Thebelt et al. 2021) and Misic tree encoding; contrasts with GP-based ParEGO/TSEMO and NSGA-II, the only rival run (pp. 4, 8, 10, 15).
writing: Problem framed from energy-systems needs before method; benefits attributed to sample efficiency, categorical handling and constraints (pp. 3-4, 30).
limits_future: MIQP does not scale well with data and dimension; time limit only on own method; only bi-objective cases tested; future applications with more objectives (pp. 14-16, 30).

method_links.note: Trained tree ensemble written as MIP constraints and optimised with input constraints; BASF co-authors; code released.
Fairness protocol (same initial points, 25 seeds, default competitor settings, disclosed time-limit asymmetry), but only NSGA-II and sampling baselines are run.

transferable: Write known input constraints, including symmetry-breaking supporting constraints, into the MIP acquisition problem so every proposal is feasible (pp. 21, 25).
Give every method the same seeded initial design and report medians with quartiles over fixed seeds (pp. 15, 18).
Include a pure feasible-sampling baseline to separate the value of feasibility from the value of the surrogate (p. 24).
Compare with the source benchmark's published best to show what a continuous formulation buys (p. 25).
coauthors: Alexander Thebelt (first author), Calvin Tsay, Robert M. Lee (BASF), Nathan Sudermann-Merx, David Walz (BASF), Tom Tranter (UCL)

quotes.text: We note that this procedure only affects the method presented here, and not other tools that we compare against.
Based on preliminary studies we found that the performance of different algorithms is highly dependent on the quality of the initial population.

title: ROmodel: modeling robust optimization problems in Pyomo
contribution: Open-source Pyomo extension (UncParam, UncSet, AdjustableVar) with reformulation, cutting-plane and nominal solvers, automatic recognition of uncertainty-set geometry, and an extension interface demonstrated with (warped) GP uncertainty sets on six case studies (read: arXiv v1).
problem_entry: Many robust-optimisation variants and required expertise discourage practitioners; no common platform to compare approaches; existing tools are solvers or tied to Julia (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Model robust problems in close analogy to the math inside Pyomo; reformulation solver detects set geometry per constraint and applies the matching transformation; new sets/reformulations plug in via library classes and _check_applicability/_reformulate (pp. 4-14).
assumptions: Uncertain constraints must match a known geometry to be reformulated; cutting planes need convex sets and suitable solvers; GP sets decision-dependent and linear in the uncertain parameter; only linear decision rules (pp. 8-13).
experiments: Six case studies (portfolio, knapsack, pooling, facility location, GP-priced production planning, drill scheduling), 30 set sizes each; median times reformulation 74 ms vs cuts 330 ms, cuts better on pooling-ellipsoidal and facility; transformation median 3.2 ms; conservatism by set geometry (pp. 14-17).
positioning: Modelling layer versus robust solvers ROME, RSOME, ROC++, PyROS; closest to JuMPeR but tied more tightly to its modelling language; open versus AIMMS (pp. 2-3).
writing: Three numbered aims, then code listings for every object; conclusion of two sentences (pp. 2, 4-8, 17).
limits_future: Not every modelled set can be solved; only linear decision rules; positioned as a prototyping and comparison platform (pp. 6, 8, 17).

method_links.note: Rival reformulations and uncertainty sets become switchable options behind one modelling interface; GPy-trained GPs enter the model as uncertainty sets.
Automatic recognition of uncertainty-set geometry before applying a transformation.
Per-class verdict: reformulation faster overall, cutting planes better on nonconvex pooling with ellipsoidal sets and on facility location.

transferable: Design the extension interface as detect-applicability plus reformulate so new reformulations plug in without touching models (p. 13).
Report solver time and the layer's own transformation time separately (p. 16).
Ship every case study as an importable example so results are one call away (p. 14).

quotes.text: However, not every set that can be modeled with Pyomo constraints can necessarily also be solved.
The reformulation solver generally outperforms the cutting plane solver with median times of 74ms and 330ms respectively.

title: An optimization approach coupling preprocessing with model regression for enhanced chemometrics
contribution: Optimises spectral preprocessing parameters and the number of PLS latent variables jointly with ENTMOOT, for accuracy or a new moment-matching robustness metric against known variability sources, checked by complete enumeration on simulated and NIR/Raman data.
problem_entry: Preprocessing is chosen by trial and error before PLS, missing the synergy between the steps; model selection uses accuracy (RMSEP) alone (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Decision vector u = (SG window, polynomial order, derivative order, latent variables); robustness = weighted sum of pairwise distances of prediction means and variances across realisations of a known nuisance factor (pp. 4-6).
assumptions: Unimodal outputs; nuisance realisations uncorrelated with other variation and categorical; similar concentration levels across classes; beta weight set by trial and error; small integer grid enabling enumeration (pp. 4-5, 7, 11).
experiments: Simulated example and two NIR/Raman literature datasets; ENTMOOT with 90 initial points and 200 iterations; accuracy models up to seven latent variables vs one or two for robustness; complete enumeration agrees except one case within 1%; random-split sensitivity and extra test sets (pp. 7-15).
positioning: Places PLS preprocessing selection within hyperparameter optimisation (grid/random search, BO); contrasts with sequential DoE and genetic-algorithm selection (pp. 1-2).
writing: Two-fold scope-and-novelty statement; simple simulated example first to build intuition before industrial data (pp. 2, 8-9).
limits_future: Robust models sometimes less accurate; only extreme objectives optimised, trade-off left open; more preprocessing steps and their order; decomposition for scale; third example code withheld for confidentiality (pp. 7, 15-16).

method_links.note: Black-box optimiser answers independently checked by complete enumeration on a deliberately coarsened domain.
In-house tree-ensemble optimiser ENTMOOT reused on an industrial partner's problem.
Two extremes (accuracy, robustness) each optimised but the interpolating family is not built; trade-off left as future work.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: validate a black-box optimiser by complete enumeration on a coarsened domain
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Window-size step of 5 chosen so enumeration is feasible; enumeration confirms ENTMOOT optima except one case within 1%.

transferable: Turn robustness to a known nuisance factor into a loss by matching prediction means and variances across nuisance levels (pp. 4-5).
Choose the decision grid so complete enumeration stays feasible and report where BO and enumeration disagree (pp. 7, 15).
Hold out an entire nuisance level (keeping the middle one in training) to test which model complexity still predicts it (p. 9).
coauthors: Chrysoula D. Kappatou (first author), James Odgers (Imperial), Salvador Garcia-Munoz (Eli Lilly)

quotes.text: Complete enumeration serves here as a validation tool to ensure successful termination of the ENTMOOT solver.
However, this comes in some cases together with an inferior performance in terms of model prediction.
